book: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology, 4th ed. (Rizzo)
kicker: Lesson 16 of your course, built from Chapter 16 of your Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology textbook (Rizzo). Test practice uses checked answers, because there is no official key for this test.

steps.title: What digestion does
teach: The digestive system breaks food (complex carbohydrates, proteins and fats) into simpler nutrients by hydrolysis, using water and enzymes. This lets cells turn food energy into ATP.

Five basic activities: ingestion (taking food in), peristalsis (pushing food along the tract), digestion (mechanical and chemical breakdown), absorption (passing digested food into the blood and lymph) and defecation (eliminating what can’t be digested or absorbed).
The enzymes: amylase turns complex carbohydrates into simple sugars; proteases turn proteins into amino acids; lipases turn fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

act.prompt: Which enzyme breaks down each food?

items.label: Starch and glycogen into simple sugars

steps.title: The alimentary canal and accessory organs
teach: The gastrointestinal tract (alimentary canal) is a tube about 30 feet long from mouth to anus: mouth, oropharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine.
The accessory structures are the teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver and gallbladder, and pancreas. Food doesn’t pass through most of them; they help digest it.

steps.title: The four tunics of the tract
teach: From the esophagus to the anal canal, the walls have the same four layers, called tunics.
Tunica mucosa (innermost): a mucous membrane of epithelium, the lamina propria (loose connective tissue underneath) and the muscularis mucosa. It protects, secretes and absorbs.

Tunica submucosa: loose connective tissue binding the mucosa to the muscularis. Tunica muscularis: inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle that churns and propels food (skeletal muscle in the mouth, pharynx and upper esophagus). Tunica serosa (adventitia), the outermost: the visceral peritoneum; an extension of it forms the mesentery.

act.prompt: Put the tunics in order from the inside out.

steps.title: The mouth and tongue
teach: The mouth (buccal cavity) has the cheeks at the sides, the hard and soft palates as its roof and the tongue as its floor. The uvula hangs from the soft palate and stops food going up into the nose when you swallow.
The tongue is skeletal muscle covered with mucous membrane, attached to the hyoid. Papillae give it a rough surface; fungiform and circumvallate papillae have taste buds.
The five tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Umami, identified by Japanese researchers, detects monosodium glutamate (MSG).

act.prompt: Which structure hangs from the soft palate?

steps.title: Saliva and the salivary glands
teach: Small buccal glands in the lining of the mouth secrete a little saliva. Most comes from three pairs of large glands: the parotid, submandibular (submaxillary) and sublingual.

Saliva is 99.5% water. It also has chloride (activates amylase), amylase (starts breaking down starch and glycogen), bicarbonate and phosphate buffers (pH 6.35 to 6.85), mucin (lubricates) and lysozyme (kills bacteria).
Mumps is a viral infection of the salivary glands, especially the parotids.

act.prompt: What does each part of saliva do?

steps.title: Teeth
teach: Chewing is mastication. Children have 20 deciduous teeth; adults have 32 permanent teeth: 8 incisors (cut), 4 canines or cuspids (tear), 8 premolars or bicuspids and 12 molars (grind).

A tooth has a crown above the gum, a neck and one to three roots. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body. Beneath is dentin, around the pulp cavity; root canals lead down to the apical foramen, where vessels and nerves enter. Cementum covers the root and attaches it to the periodontal ligament.
Dental caries (cavities) form when bacteria turn food residue into acid that dissolves enamel.

steps.title: Swallowing and the esophagus
teach: Swallowing is deglutition. The tongue forms a bolus and pushes it to the oropharynx (voluntary). Then, involuntarily, the soft palate and uvula close off the nasopharynx, and the larynx rises to the epiglottis to seal the airway. The bolus enters the esophagus.

The esophagus is a collapsible muscular tube behind the trachea, about 10 inches long. It passes through the diaphragm at the esophageal hiatus. It doesn’t digest or absorb; it secretes mucus and moves food by peristalsis. The lower esophageal (gastroesophageal) sphincter controls entry to the stomach.
A hiatal hernia lets part of the stomach push up through the diaphragm, often causing acid reflux (heartburn).

options.label: Peristalsis
options.feedback: That’s the wave-like movement that pushes food along.

steps.title: The stomach
teach: The J-shaped stomach has four parts: the cardia (around the gastroesophageal sphincter), the fundus (rounded top), the body (middle) and the pylorus (the narrow inferior region connecting to the duodenum through the pyloric sphincter).
Empty, its lining folds into rugae, which smooth out as it fills. It has three smooth muscle layers (oblique, circular and longitudinal) for churning.

Gastric glands have three secreting cells: chief (zymogenic) cells secrete pepsinogen; parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid, which turns pepsinogen into pepsin to start protein digestion; mucous cells secrete protective mucus. The stomach empties in 2 to 6 hours. It absorbs some water, salts, aspirin and alcohol.
Ulcers form when acid and enzymes erode the lining; the bacterium Helicobacter pylori is linked to most.

steps.title: The pancreas
teach: The pancreas sits below the stomach and connects to the duodenum by the pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung), which usually joins the common bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.

Its acini cells are exocrine: they release pancreatic juice, a mix of digestive enzymes (lipases, carbohydrases and proteases); duct cells add sodium bicarbonate. Its islets are endocrine: alpha cells make glucagon and beta cells make insulin.

act.prompt: Which pancreatic cells release the digestive enzymes of pancreatic juice?

steps.title: The liver and gallbladder
teach: The liver is one of the largest organs of the digestive system, about 4 pounds, with right and left lobes made of lobules.

Six main jobs: it makes heparin and clotting proteins; its Kupffer cells (liver macrophages) eat bacteria and worn-out blood cells; it detoxifies poisons and converts toxic ammonia into urea; it stores excess glucose as glycogen or fat; it stores glycogen, iron, copper and vitamins A, D, E and K; and it makes bile salts to emulsify fats.

The gallbladder, a pear-shaped sac in a depression on the liver’s surface, stores and concentrates bile, releasing it into the duodenum through the common bile duct. Gallstones form when cholesterol precipitates in the bile.

steps.title: The small intestine
teach: The small intestine is about 21 feet long. Its parts: the duodenum (first and shortest, about 10 inches), the jejunum (about 8 feet) and the ileum (about 12 feet), which joins the large intestine at the ileocecal valve.
Intestinal glands secrete enzymes; duodenal (Brunner’s) glands and goblet cells secrete alkaline mucus to neutralize acidic chyme (the semifluid contents).

About 80% of nutrient absorption happens here. The surface is huge thanks to plicae (folds), 4 to 5 million villi and microvilli. Each villus has capillaries that pick up sugars and amino acids and a lacteal that picks up fats.

act.prompt: Put the parts of the small intestine in order.

steps.title: The large intestine
teach: The large intestine (bowel) is about 5 feet long. It absorbs water, makes and absorbs some vitamins and forms and expels feces.

Regions: the cecum (pouch with the appendix attached), the colon (ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid, made of pouches called haustrae), the rectum and the anal canal, guarded by internal and external sphincters.
Gut bacteria make vitamin K, biotin and vitamin B5. Mass peristalsis drives contents into the rectum, triggering the defecation reflex. More fiber makes softer stools.

act.prompt: Put the large intestine regions in order.

steps.title: Vitamins and essential nutrients
teach: There are six classes of nutrients: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins, minerals and water. Essential nutrients are those we must get from food because the body can’t make enough of them.

Vitamin A: vision, bone growth and epithelial cells. Vitamin B1 (thiamine): muscle and nerve function; deficiency causes beriberi. B2, B3 (niacin, part of NAD), B5, B6 and B12 support energy metabolism. Vitamin C: antioxidant; deficiency causes scurvy. Vitamin D: bone mineralization. Vitamin E: protects vitamin A and fatty acids. Vitamin K: blood clotting.

steps.title: Digestive disorders
teach: Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver (viral or from alcohol); hepatitis A spreads through contaminated food and water, hepatitis B through blood and sexual contact. Jaundice is yellowing from bile pigment.
Cirrhosis is long-term liver degeneration in which the lobes become covered with fibrous connective tissue, most often from chronic alcohol abuse.
Others in the chapter: appendicitis, ulcers, gallstones, hiatal hernia, dental caries and mumps. Thrush is a fungal infection of the mouth (it’s not related to rectal veins, which are hemorrhoids).

quiz.q: Composed of loose connective tissue, the underlying layer of the mucus membrane is called the __________________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the layer of loose connective tissue under the mucosal epithelium is the lamina propria. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The ___________________ glands in the mucous membrane lining the mouth secrete small amounts of saliva.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the mucous membrane lining the mouth contains small buccal glands that secrete small amounts of saliva. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: Swallowing is also called ______________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says swallowing is called deglutition. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The ______________ cells release a mixture of digestive enzymes, collectively called the pancreatic juice.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the acini release a mixture of digestive enzymes called pancreatic juice. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The lobes of a liver affected by _____________________ are covered with fibrous connective tissue.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says in cirrhosis the lobes of the liver are covered with fibrous connective tissue. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The _______________ is one of the largest organs in the digestive system.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the liver is one of the largest organs of the digestive system. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The crown of a tooth is covered by _________________, the hardest substance in the body.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: Vitamin _______ is necessary for vision, bone growth and maintenance of epithelial cells.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says vitamin A is necessary for vision, bone growth and maintenance of epithelial cells. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The enzyme that breaks down fats into fatty acids and glycerol is _______________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says lipases break fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The passage of digested food from the digestive tract into the cardiovascular and lymphatic systems is called __________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 defines absorption as the passage of digested food from the digestive tract into the cardiovascular and lymphatic systems. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: Vitamin _______ is also known as thiamine and is necessary for muscle and nerve function.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says vitamin B1, thiamine, is necessary for muscle and nerve function. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The collapsible, muscular tube that is situated behind the trachea is called the ________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the esophagus is a collapsible, muscular tube situated behind the trachea. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The first part of the small intestine is called the ____________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the duodenum is the first and shortest part of the small intestine. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The __________________ converts harmful ammonia from the digestion of proteins to harmless urea and provides bile to emulsify fats.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the liver converts toxic ammonia to urea and produces bile salts to emulsify fats. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: Liver macrophages are called _______________ cells.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says Kupffer cells of the liver phagocytize bacteria and worn-out blood cells. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: Hydrochloric acid is secreted into the stomach by _________________ cells.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: Pepsinogen is secreted by ______________ cells.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the zymogenic or chief cells secrete pepsinogen. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The taste of ________________ detects monosodium glutamate.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the umami taste detects MSG (monosodium glutamate). Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The walls of the alimentary canal have a similar arrangement of tissue layers called ______________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the walls of the alimentary canal have the same arrangement of tissue layers, called coats or tunics. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: Complex carbohydrates are digested into simple sugars by _______________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says amylase breaks complex carbohydrates into simple sugars. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The physical movement or pushing of food along the digestive tract is called ____________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 defines peristalsis as the physical movement or pushing of food along the digestive tract. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The innermost layer of the alimentary canal is called the tunica _________________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the tunica mucosa is the innermost lining of the canal. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: Hanging from the posterior border of the soft palate is a cone-shaped muscular structure called the _____________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the uvula is a cone-shaped muscular structure hanging from the posterior border of the soft palate. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The narrow inferior region of the stomach is called the _________________.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the pylorus is the narrow inferior region of the stomach. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The __________________, located in a depression of the surface of the liver, stores bile.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the gallbladder is located in a depression on the surface of the liver and stores bile. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: Essential nutrients are nutrients a person must obtain from food because the body cannot manufacture them in sufficient amounts to meet its physiological needs.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 defines essential nutrients this way. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: Digestion allows the body’s cells to convert food energy into the high-energy ATP molecules that run the cell’s machinery.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says digestion allows the body’s cells to convert food energy into ATP. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: Thrush is caused by inflammation and enlargement of rectal veins.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 describes thrush as a fungal infection of the mouth. Inflamed, enlarged rectal veins are hemorrhoids. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The accessory structures of the alimentary canal include the oral cavity, oropharynx, esophagus, and stomach.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Those are parts of the alimentary canal itself. The accessory structures are the teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.

quiz.q: The empty stomach lining has many folds called rugae that allow the stomach to expand and hold large amounts of food.
quiz.e: Checked answer, not from an official key. Chapter 16 says the empty stomach’s mucosa lies in large folds called rugae that smooth out as it fills. Source: Fundamentals of Anatomy and Physiology (Rizzo), Chapter 16.
